Amazon A-to-z: First Claim
Resume

Amazon · A-to-z First Claim

A warning could explain the penalty and still leave a seller lost.

A first-claim email told sellers about a penalty without making the next action clear. I championed coverage for eligible first claims and redesigned the email to explain the stakes and prevent a repeat.

Role
UX Designer II, Amazon Seller Central
Scope
Seller research, coverage proposal, claims-process mapping, and first-claim email
Key decision
Cover eligible first claims under $50 and use the event to teach prevention
Outcome
Reported higher seller confidence and lower A-to-z support-call volume after 60 days in the U.S.

I — Inspiration

Support contacts showed what sellers did not understand

The first-claim notification arrived at a difficult moment: a customer had been refunded, an account metric was at stake, and the seller needed to decide what to do. Explaining that something had gone wrong was only the beginning. The message also needed to make the next action understandable.

When a customer’s order from a third-party seller goes wrong and the seller does not respond in time, Amazon steps in. The customer gets a refund. The seller gets an A-to-z claim, a hit to Order Defect Rate, and an email that often felt like discipline.

I reviewed 250 Seller Support contacts tied to A-to-z. Appeals, disputes, and status questions accounted for a substantial share; the analysis marked many of them preventable. The opportunity was to explain the process before a confused seller needed support.

D — Design Process

Sellers needed an explanation, not another warning

I mapped messaging, eligibility, disputes, and appeals with stakeholders and domain experts. Seller interviews showed that actions were unclear, Order Defect Rate mattered deeply, and sellers lacked confidence they could avoid the next claim.

I aligned partners on three tenets: use the first claim as a learning opportunity, inform rather than discipline, and help sellers prevent a repeat. Those tenets changed the structure of the notification, not just its tone.

E — Engagement

Give the program a shared teaching purpose

The tenets gave partners a shared basis for evaluating the email against seller needs. The notification also had to reflect the wider program accurately: an encouraging tone could not substitute for precise expectations about coverage and Order Defect Rate.

I championed Amazon-funded coverage and brought a proposal to leadership, legal, finance, and other partners. Investigating a first claim could cost as much as or more than the claim itself; I proposed using that investment to resolve the customer’s issue quickly and teach the seller. This was advocacy and feasibility work, not sole policy or budget authority.

A — Action

I rebuilt the email around what sellers needed to know

Coverage applied to eligible first claims strictly under $50, with circumstance-specific limitations. The email had to explain that boundary clearly. I structured the email around four jobs: explain the claim, make Order Defect Rate understandable, state eligible first-claim coverage, and give practical prevention steps. The stakes stayed visible while the message became useful to act on.

The hierarchy makes each job inspectable

Claim details first
Name the current event and give the seller a clear route to inspect it.
Expectations
Explain the account metric before offering guidance.
Eligible coverage
Identify the strict under-$50 limit and circumstance-specific restrictions.
Prevention
Give practical actions the seller can take before another claim.

S — Success

After launch, sellers reported more confidence

88%
Of email openers reported confidence in avoiding future claims
14%
Reported reduction in A-to-z-related support-call volume

Reported results, 60 days after the U.S. launch. Retrospective results have not been independently revalidated.

Seller-initiated refunds were also reported as trending toward a 30% year-over-year increase. These are program-level results, not an isolated test of the email.

My takeaway: first-claim coverage created room to teach. Specific explanations and prevention steps made that investment useful to the seller.
